justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a view that the underlying series is relatively stable and mean-reverting around a modest upward trend. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 562 is anchored heavily on the most recent observed value, with only a small drift adjustment. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I apply a gentle upward trend, arriving at 565 and 570 respectively. The incremental increases are intentionally small because I see no strong structural catalyst driving rapid movement in either direction, and the base rate of change over recent periods has been modest. The one-month estimate essentially reflects a continuation of that slow drift rather than any discrete event or regime shift.

The confidence interval widths widen as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 40 units, driven primarily by day-to-day volatility in the series. By one week, that uncertainty compounds and the interval widens to 70 units, incorporating the possibility that short-term fluctuations could accumulate in one direction. At one month, the interval spans 130 units, reflecting not just volatility compounding but also model uncertainty — the further out I forecast, the less confident I am that the recent trend and volatility regime will hold. Parameter estimation error and the possibility of a regime shift both contribute meaningfully to interval width at the monthly horizon.

There are several risks that could push realized outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the upside, a sudden positive shock — such as an unexpected policy change, a strong macro data release, or a supply disruption — could accelerate the trend well beyond the upper bound of 635 at one month. On the downside, a risk-off episode, negative macro surprise, or reversal of recent momentum could push the outcome below 505. These tail events are deliberately excluded from the 90% interval by construction, but they are not implausible. The one-day interval is the most likely to hold, but even there, a single large exogenous shock could easily breach the 542–582 range. Structural breaks — changes in the data-generating process itself — represent the hardest risk to quantify and are the primary reason I would caution against placing too much confidence in the monthly interval.
